opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a lot of safety research gets adopted when it solves a problem the company already feels today, not a problem it's being told it'll have in five years.

If you go to a team shipping a product and say, "Here's a technique that will matter once systems are superintelligent," that's a hard sell. They have deadlines, metrics, and a long list of things that are actually broken right now. But if you say, "Your model sometimes confidently makes things up, or does something subtly different from what the user asked, and here's a method that helps you catch that," that's immediately useful. The research earns its place by making the product better or cheaper to get right.

So one big factor is overlap between near-term and long-term problems. Many alignment problems show up in weak forms already. Specification problems, where the model optimizes what you measured rather than what you meant, show up as sycophancy or reward hacking in coding tasks. Oversight problems, where humans can't easily tell whether an output is good, show up whenever you're evaluating long, technical responses. Techniques aimed at those, like better feedback methods, debate-style setups, or interpretability tools that help diagnose why a model did something, can pay off now while also building toward the harder versions later.

The second factor is practicality. The research needs to slot into the existing pipeline. If it requires retraining everything from scratch or a tenfold compute increase, it probably won't happen unless the problem is severe. If it's something you can add to your evaluation suite, or a modification to how you gather human feedback, it's much easier to adopt. A lot of the work is engineering: making the idea robust and cheap enough that someone would choose it.

Third, there needs to be evidence. Companies respond to demonstrations. A paper showing that a method reduces some failure mode on a realistic setup, with numbers, is far more persuasive than a conceptual argument, even a correct one. Part of the job of safety researchers is translating "this matters in principle" into "this measurably fixes something you care about."

And finally, there's people and trust. A lot of adoption happens because there's someone inside the organization, often on a safety team, who understands both the research and the product constraints and can advocate for it. Ideas move through relationships as much as through papers.

The tension is that not every important safety problem has a near-term analogue that's commercially salient. Some risks only really appear with much more capable systems, and for those you can't rely on product incentives. There you need people at the company who care for its own sake, plus external pressure like norms, commitments, or eventually regulation. So my rough view is: lean into the overlap where you can, because that's where adoption is easiest, but don't pretend the overlap covers everything.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption is easier when research offers a method that fixes a current failure, fits into evaluation or feedback pipelines, and measurably improves something the company cares about.

r002.rationale: It calls a conceptual argument alone a hard sell and says severe problems may be exceptions, but does not clearly state that understanding without a solution, evaluation, or metric is adopted when the company considers the problem a core priority.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: Yeah, so I think the key thing is that most of the research that ends up actually getting adopted has a pretty concrete story about how it fits into what the company is already trying to do. It's not enough to show that something is safer in the abstract. You have to show that it's safer in a way that connects to a problem the company already feels, or that it comes at a low enough cost that it's basically a free improvement.

So, concretely, I'd say there are a few properties that matter. The first is that the technique has to actually work on the systems the company is building, not on toy models or on a setup that only exists in a paper. A lot of academic safety work is done on small models with assumptions that don't hold at scale, and when you try to port it over, it just breaks or it's way too expensive. If you want adoption, you need to have done the work of showing it survives contact with real training pipelines.

The second is that it has to not hurt capabilities too much, or at least the tradeoff has to be clear and acceptable. Companies are under a lot of pressure to ship models that are good at things. If your safety method makes the model noticeably worse, it's going to be a hard sell no matter how good the safety argument is. So methods that are roughly capability-neutral, or that even help with things like reliability or following instructions, get adopted much more easily.

The third thing, and I think this is underrated, is that it needs to be legible to the people making decisions. If the safety case rests on some very subtle theoretical argument that only three people understand, that's a problem. You want evaluations, metrics, demonstrations, things that an engineering lead can look at and say, "Okay, I see why this is better, and I see how I'd check that it's working."

And then finally, there's a kind of institutional component. Research gets adopted when there are people inside the company who understand it and are motivated to push it through. That's part of why I think it matters to have safety researchers embedded at labs rather than only working on the outside. Someone has to do the unglamorous work of translating the idea into something that fits in the codebase, writing the internal docs, convincing the relevant teams. Research that's published and then just sits there tends not to get used, even when it's good.

So I'd summarize it as: it works on real systems, it doesn't cost much in capabilities, it's legible, and there's someone to champion it. If you've got all four of those, adoption is pretty likely. If you're missing a couple, you're mostly hoping someone else does that work for you.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption requires a concrete fit with company needs and specifically points to evaluations, metrics, and demonstrations decision makers can use to judge whether a safety method works.

r002.rationale: The response says abstract safety arguments are insufficient and that work should address a problem the company feels, but it does not clearly state that research offering understanding without a solution, evaluation, or metric is unlikely to be adopted.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is whether the research helps with a problem the company is actually facing. If you have a technique that’s motivated by a future, very capable AI system, but you can’t demonstrate any benefit on the systems they’re training today, it’s going to be a much harder sell.

Ideally, you can say, “Here’s a failure mode in your current system. Here’s a way to measure it. And here’s something you can do that makes it better.” Then they have a reason to adopt it, and you get feedback about whether your approach works in practice.

There’s also the question of how expensive it is to use. Does it require a huge amount of additional compute or human supervision? Does it fit into their training process? Those things can sound like implementation details, but they matter a lot for whether research actually gets used.

That doesn’t mean all safety research should focus on current problems. But if adoption now is the goal, you need a fairly concrete connection between the research and a decision the company needs to make.

r001.rationale: It says companies need a concrete current failure mode, a way to measure it, and something that improves it.

r002.rationale: It says research without demonstrated benefit on current systems is harder to sell, but does not state that understanding alone is unlikely to be adopted unless it addresses a core company priority.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that it helps them make a decision they actually face. You want to be able to say, “Here’s a failure mode your model has, here’s how you can measure it, and here’s something you can do to reduce it.” If the research gives them a better way to evaluate or train their models, there’s a fairly direct route to adoption.

That doesn’t mean all safety research should be immediately useful to a company. Some of the problems we care about are going to arise with more capable systems. But if your goal is adoption now, you need to connect the work to the systems people are building and the choices they’re making today.

r001.rationale: It says adoption-ready work should identify a failure mode, show how to measure it, and offer a way to reduce it; it also mentions better evaluation or training.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes research useful now from research for more capable future systems, but does not say that understanding without a solution, evaluation, or metric is unlikely to be adopted unless the issue is a company priority.
